introduction.text: The Arch of Janus is the only surviving quadrifrons triumphal arch in Rome, notable for its unique four‑fronted design and uncertain purpose, which may have served as a boundary marker, shelter for traders, or a monument to a Roman emperor.

history.description: Constructed in the early 4th century AD as a quadrifrons arch at the northeastern limit of the Forum Boarium, possibly serving as a boundary marker or shelter for traders.
In 1830, the attic storey was removed, mistakenly believed to be non‑original, altering the arch's appearance.
Since the explosion of a bomb on 27 July 1993 in front of San Giorgio in Velabro, the arch has been inaccessible to the public.
Built using spolia, including bricks and pottery shards, and covered with white marble from earlier buildings.
In the Middle Ages, the Frangipane family transformed the arch into a fortress, preserving it until the 19th century.

design.description: The arch is a quadrifrons structure with four arches and four facades, each pier featuring two rows of three niches.
The keystone at the apex of the central arch on the north side is thought to depict Minerva, though some scholars suggest it represents the Palladium.
The arch originally had an attic storey, which was removed in 1830, and a staircase within the north‑west pier that would have provided access to the top floor.

art.description: The keystone of the central arch may depict the goddess Minerva, indicating a possible artistic representation of a deity.
The arch contains 48 niches that could have housed statues, though none have been identified.
